subject: Follow-up: token economics & continuous-batching assumptions for Avery Health integration
messages:

Subject: Quick recap + token/unit-econ worksheet (post-discovery)

Hi Sara — great call today, thanks for walking us through the Avery Health use case. Quick recap and next steps so we keep momentum: 

Key items we captured:
- Primary workload: patient-facing summarization + triage assistant (short dialogue history).
- Expected live users (pilot): 50k–150k monthly active; peak concurrency during morning triage windows.
- Latency target: ~300ms p50 for triage responses (critical).
- Quality target: clinically-safe output + consistent formatting.

Pricing & volume questions (to finalize unit economics):
1) Can you confirm average tokens per generated response (rough ballpark is fine)?
2) Expected messages per user per month (notifications / triage events)?
3) Target budget range expressed as $/1M tokens or monthly budget band? You mentioned being sensitive to $/1M — what’s your target?

I attached a short token-econ worksheet that we use to model effective $/1M under different batching and concurrency assumptions. I’ll sketch a conservative baseline and a batched baseline once you confirm the bullets above.

Next steps I propose:
- You reply with the three items above (tokens, messages/user, target $/1M).
- We share a modeled worksheet and a 30-minute follow-up to review (we have availability Thursday/Friday this week).

Attachments: [Attachment: redwood-token-econ-worksheet.xlsx (XLSX, 42KB)]

Thanks — will keep Marissa and Priyom in the loop for pricing and infra details.

—Sean

Subject: Re: Quick recap + token/unit-econ worksheet (post-discovery)

Thanks Sean — great summary. A few quick clarifications: 

- Average tokens per generated response: ~200–240 tokens (we measured on our test set; some longer summaries reach ~400 tokens but are <5% of volume).
- Messages per user per month: 6–9 (mix of notifications and triage hits).
- Target $/1M tokens: we’re aiming for ~ $220–$280 to start (depends on SLA/throughput guarantees).

On batching/concurrency: our traffic pattern is spiky — big morning window (07:30–09:30) with 40–60 concurrent requests, then low steady-state the rest of the day (5–10 concurrency). How much can we rely on continuous-batching savings vs. peak provisioning? If batching adds tail latency that pushes past 300ms p50, we’ll need a fallback plan.

Procurement: Our procurement team will want an estimated monthly spend for pilot scale (number of users × messages × avg tokens). If you can include an example table in your worksheet that maps tokens → estimated monthly cost under both conservative and batched assumptions, that would be ideal.

Thanks,
Sara
Sara Jenkins
Product Lead, Avery Health
From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwood.com>

Date: Tue, 2 Nov 2026 08:12:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Quick recap + token/unit-econ worksheet (post-discovery)

Sara — thanks, this is super helpful. Based on your ranges I sketched two modeled rows in the attached worksheet: conservative (no batching applied) and continuous-batching (realistic compression at your observed request sizes). High-level numbers below are meant as an initial calibration — we’ll refine after you confirm the pilot user count and messages/user.

Example rough model (pilot = 75k MAU, 7 msg/user/month, avg generated tokens = 220):
- Raw tokens/month = 75,000 * 7 * 220 = ~115.5M tokens
- Conservative $/1M (no batching): $300 → monthly = $34,650
- Continuous-batching adjusted (assume 1.9× token-efficiency at typical QPS) → effective tokens billed = 115.5M / 1.9 ≈ 60.8M → at $260/1M = $15,808

Notes/assumptions: 
- The 1.9× compression estimate assumes continuous batching across many small requests during the morning peak and prefix caching for repeated snippets. We modeled a conservative 1.5× and an optimistic 2.2× in the worksheet.
- To preserve p50 ≤ 300ms we recommend a hybrid policy: short batch window (8–12ms) + priority routing for high-SLA calls (no batching or smaller batch size). That keeps tail latency low while letting the bulk of traffic benefit from batching.
- We included a line showing cost/savings at different target $/1M to match procurement scenarios you asked about.

Attachments: [Attachment: redwood-token-econ-worksheet.xlsx (XLSX, 42KB)]
Related: https://app.hubspot.com/deal/9821

Proposed next step: 30-minute follow-up Thursday Nov 4 to review the worksheet and walk procurement through the example monthly estimate. Is 10–11am ET open for you?

—Sean

Sara — quick technical addendum on continuous batching and latency tradeoffs based on our past pilots: 

1) Batching behaviour by QPS: at low QPS (<10 rps) batching windows rarely collect >2 requests; efficiency gains are small. During your morning peak (40–60 concurrent requests) we typically see batching pack 6–10 requests per model step which drives the 1.7–2.2× token efficiency range.

2) Tail-latency controls: the short batch window I recommended (8–12ms) is tuned so that p50 is largely unaffected; p95 can increase slightly. For strict p50 SLAs we use a two-tier queue: latency-sensitive requests goto a low-latency path (smaller batches / reserved GPU slices), bulk requests use the batching path.

3) Streaming vs final-chunk: if you stream partial tokens to the client, perceived latency improves even when batching is happening; that’s a common pattern for clinical triage where UX tolerates incremental text.

4) Empirical example (pilot-like run): avg gen tokens 220, QPS peak 55, observed batching compression 1.85×, median generation latency (batched) ~210ms, median (low-latency path) ~160ms. See attached latency map for a visual: [Attachment: map-batching-latency.png (PNG, 88KB)].

Happy to run a 1-hour profiling run against your test set once we have API access — we’ll produce a short report showing expected cost and latency under your exact traffic curve.

—Priyom
